cells.tense: You are choosing the next step from what you can actually see, right here.
cells.ask: Write down tomorrow's one next step, and one thing you won't do, and keep both.
cells.core:
You know what you're pointed at, and you know what you're not doing. The fog isn't a problem to solve before moving. You take the step that's visible and leave the rest of the road alone. The direction holds without you squeezing it.

What makes this last is staying with the choice while it unfolds, without forcing it to be finished. That's the balance — moving without white-knuckling, clear without needing the ending in advance. You can hold a decision and let it stay a decision, not a verdict to enforce. It survives a bad week because it isn't braced against one. Keep choosing at the pace the fog allows, and the pace stays yours.

cells.tense: You are bracing against a future that hasn't been written yet.
cells.ask: Let one thing you're pushing stay unforced for a day, and notice what it does on its own.
cells.core:
You're trying to see the whole road before you take the first step, and you're steering by what might happen instead of what's here. That's not focus — it's force. The pushing to nail down an outcome is costing you the very thing the pushing was for.

Recognition, not a verdict, is what loosens it. You can want it to land and still not grip it. See the pattern whole, and keep it open. When you stop writing the ending in advance, you find you're choosing from what's in front of you — and the fog is workable instead of something to defeat. Hands come off the wheel at the joint you'd otherwise lock.

cells.tense: You are still at a door that closed behind you.
cells.ask: Take one small action on one thing you keep saying doesn't matter, and don't check how it went.
cells.core:
There's a door in the past that didn't open the way it should have, and you're still there, waiting for something to change your mind. The ability to choose at all has gone quiet. Not because the direction isn't there — because the wish went behind that door too.

Nobody's asking you to push feeling back into it. The way through is the other direction: let what you actually are come forward, without needing it to prove anything. Radiance, not effort. Pick one thing you've been saying doesn't matter and take one small action on it. Not because it's important, but because you're the one who can. That's the current coming back through the wire.

cells.tense: You are holding a pen down in a room you are already writing.
cells.ask: Catch one habit you call a choice, out loud, and say 'I picked this.'
cells.core:
You think you're drifting with the current. You're actually steering — every hour, in what you give time to and go along with. You're describing what you do as something that happens to you.

The fog makes this easy to miss: when the road isn't visible, the direction you do set looks like no direction at all. That's what it looks like going well here — one step taken, the rest left alone, no grip on the ending. The bend is that you've stopped calling the steering yours. Name one habit you've been calling automatic and take it back. Not a grand redesign. One admission, one thing you actually decided.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the Too Much and Unacknowledged cells can say what the person is steering toward or what they have decided — the record says only that direction is projected onto the future or is running unowned, never where it points. A reader could reasonably say they are not steering at all, or that nothing in their life has an outcome to move. The ask survives being wrong in every cell: it is a small, finished act of local choice — a next step, one waiting, one light question, one saying-so — useful even if the read is mistaken, because it returns authorship regardless of which face is true. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person in the draft is 'You are forcing outcomes' — it turns a mechanism into an accusation and would be felt as blame; I have cut it.
